text: Services crash, deploys stall, and disks fill up quietly for days before anyone notices — resource monitoring is how you catch that before it becomes an outage, not after. This lesson covers the core command-line tools for checking CPU, memory, and disk usage on a running server.

top refreshes every few seconds and lists the most resource-hungry processes first, with CPU and memory percentages right next to each one. Northbridge Retail's ops team opens top the moment a service feels slow, before ever touching an application log, because it shows exactly what's consuming resources right now.

free -h shows memory in human-readable units, but the number that actually matters is available, not free. buff/cache is memory the kernel is using to cache disk data, and it's reclaimed instantly if an application needs it, so a server can show very little free memory while still having plenty available.

df -h shows used and free space per mounted filesystem, which tells you which disk is the problem. du -sh summarizes usage for each file or directory you point it at, and piping that through sort -rh finds the single biggest offender fast — exactly how an unrotated nginx access log got tracked down on a disk that hit ninety-three percent full.

uptime shows how long the system has been running and its load average — the average number of processes wanting CPU time over the last one, five, and fifteen minutes. A load average near or above the number of CPU cores means the system is saturated, and a rising trend, where the one-minute number is higher than the fifteen-minute one, means load is building right now.

Watching CPU, memory, and disk is what turns a developing problem into something you catch early instead of something you explain after an outage.
